1. "Recast the recurrence as a greedy scan: starting at $a_1$, an integer is accepted exactly when it is noncoprime to every previously accepted integer. This makes all accepted integers pairwise noncoprime." — This is correct: since $a_{n+1}$ must be noncoprime to all previous $a_i$, and it's the smallest integer greater than $a_n$ with this property, the sequence is exactly the greedy scan starting from $a_1$. Actually, we need to check: the greedy scan accepts an integer $m > a_1$ iff $m$ is noncoprime to every previously accepted integer. Is this the same as the given recurrence? The given recurrence says $a_{n+1}$ is the smallest integer $> a_n$ noncoprime to all of $a_1,...,a_n$. In the greedy scan, when we scan integers $a_n < m < a_{n+1}$, each such $m$ must fail to be noncoprime to all of $a_1,...,a_n$ (otherwise it would have been chosen as $a_{n+1}$... wait, no—if $m < a_{n+1}$ and $m$ is noncoprime to all $a_1,...,a_n$, then $a_{n+1}$ would be at most $m$, contradiction). So indeed, rejected integers between $a_n$ and $a_{n+1}$ are coprime to at least one of $a_1,...,a_n$. And in the greedy scan, an integer is rejected iff it's coprime to some previously accepted integer. So the two descriptions coincide. This is a correct, standard first observation.

Proof: if $m$ is not accepted, then when the scan reached $m$, it was coprime to some previously accepted integer $a_i < m$, which is an accepted integer — contradiction. Yes, correct.

3. "Finite-prime projection: every accepted integer contains a prime divisor of $a_1$..." — Correct: each $a_n$ is noncoprime to $a_1$, so shares a prime with $a_1$. Finitely many primes divide $a_1$. The "types" idea.

The observation that descending conditions need not stabilize is a valid cautionary note.
